defaults.permitted_development: Across Dorset, a new fence, wall or gate at a house is usually permitted development up to 2 metres high, or up to 1 metre where it is next to a highway used by vehicles or the footpath of such a highway. The normal right falls away where listed-building controls, Article 4 directions or relevant planning conditions apply.

rules.height_rules: Across Dorset, the main national height limits are 2 metres in most positions and 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles. Height is measured from ground level, so raised beds, retaining walls or a sloping site can change the real planning answer.
rules.depth_rules: Across Dorset, there is no separate depth allowance for fences and walls. What matters more is the line of the boundary, any change in ground level, and whether the structure starts to behave like retaining engineering rather than ordinary enclosure.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Dorset, a fence or wall is easiest to keep within householder rights when it follows an ordinary residential boundary and does not block visibility at an access or corner. Heritage constraints can also apply where the boundary relates to listed buildings or historic frontages.
rules.roof_rules: Across Dorset, fences and walls do not have a roof test, but cappings, trellis toppers, pergola-style additions or gates fixed to taller piers can all count toward the overall height and visual impact. Keep the whole boundary composition in mind rather than only the main panel height.
rules.materials_rules: Across Dorset, material choice is not controlled in the same way as height, yet it still matters. A boundary that fits the character of the house and street will usually sit more comfortably than one with overly heavy or visually harsh materials on a prominent frontage.

restrictions.conservation_area: A fence or wall in a conservation area may need more than a simple height check, especially if demolition of an older boundary is part of the scheme.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building controls can apply to fences, gates and walls where they form part of the building's curtilage or historic setting.
restrictions.article4_notes: A planning condition or Article 4 direction can override the standard boundary limits, so even a straightforward replacement fence may need consent.

rules.permitted_development: In Bournemouth Christchurch and Poole, putting up or altering a fence, wall or gate is usually simplest where the overall height stays within the normal 2 metre limit, or 1 metre by a highway used by vehicles. Heritage controls and site-specific conditions can still take the proposal outside permitted development.

rules.height_rules: For most householder boundaries the key figures are 2 metres and 1 metre by a highway used by vehicles. Ground levels matter, so a wall on top of a raised edge or planter can exceed the limit even when the panel itself looks modest.
rules.depth_rules: Depth is not usually the deciding measurement for fences and walls. The issue is more often whether the enclosure follows the normal boundary line or turns into a more substantial engineered structure with level changes behind it.
rules.boundary_rules: The enclosure may be permitted development on height, but still problematic on boundary position. Corner plots, access points, neighbouring listed curtilage and conservation-area demolition controls are all common complications.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof allowance for a fence or wall. What often catches people out is that trellis, decorative tops, coping details and gate piers can still contribute to the measured height and prominence of the boundary.
rules.materials_rules: There is no blanket requirement to copy the house materials, although front boundaries generally work better when the walling, railings or panels feel in scale with the street rather than engineered or overbearing.

restrictions.conservation_area: Conservation area status can tighten the position for boundary works, and separate consent may be needed to demolish an existing wall, fence or gate that contributes to the area's character.
restrictions.listed_building: Historic boundary walls and railings are often part of a listed building's significance, so replacement or removal can need listed building consent.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions are a common reason why an otherwise modest boundary change still needs planning permission.
